title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Ecology — 2024
subject: biology
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Define ecosystem. Describe the structure of an ecosystem with a diagram description.
questions.solution:
**Ecosystem:** organisms plus their physical environment functioning as one unit.

**Abiotic:** light, temperature, water, soil, minerals. **Biotic:** producers (plants) → primary consumers (herbivores) → secondary/tertiary consumers (carnivores) → decomposers (bacteria, fungi) recycling nutrients back to soil.

(Draw nested boxes: environment enclosing trophic levels in feeding order, decomposers arrowing back to producers.)
questions.knowledgeNote: Energy flows one way (10% rule); nutrients cycle — the two traffic laws of every ecosystem diagram.
questions.answer: **Ecosystem:** the functional unit of nature comprising a **biotic community and its abiotic environment** interacting so that energy flows (one-way, from sun through trophic levels) and matter cycles (nutrients recycle endlessly) — e.g. a pond, a grassland, a forest. **Structure (diagram description):** **abiotic components** — inorganic nutrients, water, air, light, soil; **biotic components** — **producers** (green plants/algae: grass, phytoplankton), **consumers** (herbivores: deer, zooplankton; carnivores: frog, fish; top carnivores: tiger, kingfisher), and **decomposers** (bacteria, fungi on dead matter). **Diagram description:** sun → green plants → herbivore → carnivore → top carnivore (arrow chain); every level also arrows into 'dead organic matter', which arrows into decomposers, which arrow back to the soil/water nutrient pool and thence to the plants — energy a one-way street, nutrients a roundabout. **Deep point:** draw the arrows and the lesson draws itself — matter goes round, energy goes through; the decomposer's return arrow is what keeps the roundabout turning.

questions.question: What is ecological succession? Explain with the example of xerosere.
questions.solution:
**Succession** is the ordered replacement of communities over time toward a stable climax.

**Xerosere** (bare rock → forest): lichens (pioneers, weather rock) → mosses → herbs → shrubs → forest (climax). Each stage builds soil and shade for the next.
questions.knowledgeNote: Xerosere (dry rock) vs hydrosere (open water): opposite starts, both ending in forest climax.
questions.answer: **Ecological succession:** the predictable, directional **change in community composition over time** — from bare ground through a series of seres to a stable climax, each stage modifying the environment for the next. **Xerosere (on bare rock):** (1) **crustose lichens** etch the rock and make the first soil film; (2) **foliose lichens** replace them, adding humus; (3) **mosses** establish as substrate deepens, holding moisture; (4) **herbs and grasses** oust mosses as soil thickens; (5) **shrubs** invade and shade out herbs; (6) **climax forest** — trees finally dominate the now deep, moist soil. **Deep point:** each seral stage is a landlord improving the tenement for a stronger tenant — the rock's first residents are lichens, and their rent is soil.

questions.question: Distinguish between a food chain and a food web. What is the ten percent law?
questions.solution:
**Food chain:** a single feeding line (grass → deer → tiger). **Food web:** the interlinked mesh of all chains — realistic, stable, with alternate routes if one prey fails.

**Ten percent law (Lindeman):** only ~10% of energy transfers per trophic level; the rest is lost as heat/respiration — which is why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels.
questions.knowledgeNote: Short chains feed more people per hectare — the energetics behind vegetarian efficiency arguments.
questions.answer: **Food chain:** a **linear sequence of who eats whom** — energy flowing from producers through successive consumers: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle (each link a trophic level, with ~10% of the energy passing on). **Food web:** the **interconnection of many food chains** in an ecosystem — most organisms eat and are eaten by several others, weaving the chains into a network; webs are more realistic and more **stable** (an alternative food source can compensate when one link fails). **Difference:** a chain is one line of energy flow; a web is the whole braided river of them. **Ten percent law (Lindeman):** only about **10% of the energy** entering a trophic level is transferred to the next level — the other ~90% is lost in respiration, movement, excretion and heat. Hence only ~10 kcal of every 100 kcal of plant energy reaches the herbivore, ~1 kcal the carnivore — which is why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels. **Deep point:** the ten-percent law is the reason big fierce animals are rare — energy thins out tenfold per level, so a top predator needs a very wide and productive base.

questions.question: What are ecological pyramids? Explain why the pyramid of energy is always upright.
questions.solution:
Graphic trophic structure as pyramids of **number**, **biomass**, or **energy**.

Number/biomass pyramids can invert (one tree feeding many birds; tiny phytoplankton feeding bulky zooplankton). But **energy** pyramids are always upright — each level holds only ~10% of the one below, so higher levels can never out-energy their base.
questions.knowledgeNote: Upright-energy is thermodynamically forced; inverted-number/biomass are sampling artefacts of size differences.
questions.answer: **Ecological pyramids:** graphical representations, built from the base upward, of **numbers, biomass or energy** at successive trophic levels (producers at the base, top carnivores at the apex) — showing the quantitative shape of an ecosystem. **Why the pyramid of energy is always upright:** each energy transfer between levels is inefficient — roughly **90% of the energy is lost** at every level to respiration (heat), movement and waste, so **each successive level must contain less energy than the one below**. Unlike numbers (a tree can support thousands of insects) or biomass (pond phytoplankton can be outweighed by fish at a moment), **energy cannot be inverted**: no level can contain more energy flowing through it per unit time than the level that feeds it, because energy is lost, never created, between levels. **Deep point:** numbers and biomass are photographs — capable of upside-down moments; energy is a movie of the flow, and the flow only ever runs downhill.

questions.question: Describe any three types of population interaction with one example of each.
questions.solution: **Competition** (−/−): two species lose together — weeds vs paddy. **Predation** (+/−): tiger eats deer. **Mutualism** (+/+): lichen (fungus + alga) or legume–Rhizobium. (Also: parasitism +/−, commensalism +/0, amensalism −/0.)
questions.knowledgeNote: The +/− sign code compresses every interaction into two symbols — learn it once, answer any of them.
questions.answer: **Three types of population interaction (one example each):** **(1) Mutualism (+/+):** both species benefit. *Example:* **Rhizobium in legume root nodules** — the bacterium fixes nitrogen for the plant, the plant feeds the bacterium sugars (also lichen, mycorrhiza). **(2) Predation (+/−):** one kills and eats the other. *Example:* **tiger preying on sambar deer** (also ladybird beetles eating aphids) — predation regulates prey populations and drives prey defences. **(3) Parasitism (+/−):** one lives on/in the other, harming but not immediately killing it. *Example:* ***Plasmodium*** in humans (malaria) — or *Ascaris* in the gut, Cuscuta on plants. (Also acceptable: commensalism (+/0) — epiphytic orchids on trees; competition (−/−) — *Paramecium* species in Gause's experiments.) **Deep point:** every interaction is a sign pair (+, −, 0) — the four common pairs cover the whole ecology of who benefits from whom; predation and parasitism look similar on paper but differ in tempo: the predator kills at once, the parasite harvests slowly.

questions.question: What is eutrophication? Explain its causes and effects on aquatic life.
questions.solution:
**Eutrophication** is nutrient enrichment (nitrates, phosphates from fertilisers/sewage) triggering algal blooms.

Blooms block light, then die and decompose — decomposition devours dissolved oxygen (BOD spike) → fish suffocate, biodiversity collapses, lakes turn to dead marshes.
questions.knowledgeNote: Phewa Lake's water-hyacinth choking is Nepal's textbook eutrophication case.
questions.answer: **Eutrophication:** the **over-enrichment of a water body with nutrients (nitrates and phosphates)**, leading to excessive algal/plant growth and the degradation of the aquatic ecosystem. **Causes:** (1) **fertiliser runoff** from farmland; (2) **sewage and detergent discharge** (phosphate-based detergents, untreated municipal waste); (3) **industrial effluents and animal waste** entering lakes and rivers. **Effects on aquatic life:** (1) **algal bloom** — nutrients trigger explosive algal growth, forming a surface scum that **blocks sunlight** from submerged plants; (2) **oxygen crash** — the bloom dies and sinks; decomposers consume enormous dissolved oxygen breaking it down (high BOD), **suffocating fish** and other aerobic life; (3) **anaerobic decay** — with oxygen gone, anaerobes produce H₂S, methane — the lake turns foul, toxic (some bloom algae release toxins) and ultimately lifeless below the bloom. **Deep point:** eutrophication is the lake equivalent of a feast followed by famine — nutrients first fatten the algae, then their corpses starve the water of oxygen; the fish die not of poison but of a decomposer's oxygen bill.
